pack.description: Listen and Repeat (7 sentences of increasing length) and Take an Interview (4 questions, 45 s each).
pack.copyright_policy: Original synthetic content. No operational ETS item copied.

exercises.source_reference: PRD_TOEFL_2026.md seed s_repeat_001 (item 7 shortened from ~35 to ~30 syllables)
exercises.scenario: You are training to help new students find services in the university library. Listen to your supervisor and repeat exactly what you hear.

items.text: Welcome to the library.
The information desk is downstairs.
Students can borrow laptops near the main entrance.
Please return reserved books to the desk before closing time.
If you need a quiet place to work, several study rooms are available upstairs.
Students who are preparing group presentations can reserve the media room through the library website.
Before you leave, remember that borrowed equipment must be returned to the service desk, not the book-return boxes.

exercises.scenario: You are volunteering at a university open day. Listen to the event coordinator and repeat exactly what you hear.

items.text: Tours begin at ten.
Visitors should collect a map at the entrance.
The science building is on the left side of the main square.
Parents who have questions about housing can speak to the staff in the lobby.
If a group arrives late, please take them directly to the welcome talk in the main hall.
Students who want to attend a lecture must register at the information table before eleven.
Because the east entrance is closed today, visitors with mobility needs should use the elevator behind the library.

exercises.scenario: You are starting work as an assistant in a chemistry teaching laboratory. Listen to the lab manager and repeat exactly what you hear.

items.text: Always wear your goggles.
Gloves are kept in the cabinet by the door.
Each student needs to sign the safety form before starting.
Chemical waste should never be poured into the sinks along the wall.
If anyone spills a liquid, tell them to step back and call you immediately.
The instructions for each experiment have been posted online, but printed copies are available on request.
At the end of each session, check that the gas taps are turned off and that all the equipment is back on the shelves.

exercises.scenario: You are helping at the reception desk of a student health center. Listen to the nurse and repeat exactly what you hear.

items.text: Please take a number.
The doctor will see you in a few minutes.
Remember to bring your insurance card to every appointment.
Students who feel unwell after hours can call the advice line for help.
Vaccination appointments can be booked online, although walk-in visits are also possible.
If you have been prescribed new medication, the pharmacist will explain how and when it should be taken.
Patients whose symptoms have not improved within three days should come back, even after a successful first visit.

exercises.scenario: You are participating in a university research study about students' use of artificial intelligence tools.

questions.prompt: Think about the last time you used an AI tool for studying. What did you use it for, and was it useful?
Some students prefer using AI tools alone, while others prefer discussing difficult material with classmates. Which approach works better for you and why?
Some instructors worry that frequent use of AI may reduce students' ability to think independently. Do you think this concern is justified? Why or why not?
Should universities establish common rules for how AI tools may be used in coursework, or should individual professors decide? Explain your position.

exercises.scenario: You are taking part in a study by the city transport department about how students travel to campus.

questions.prompt: How do you usually get to your classes, and how long does the journey take?
If the bus service near your home became twice as frequent, would you change the way you travel? Why or why not?
Some people believe that cities should make it more expensive to drive into the center in order to reduce traffic. What is your opinion?
Looking ahead twenty years, do you think most students will still need to travel to campus every day? Explain your view.

exercises.scenario: A researcher is interviewing students about how they balance part-time work and university studies.

questions.prompt: Have you ever had a job while studying? Describe what you did and how it affected your studies.
Would you rather have a job related to your field of study that pays less, or an unrelated job that pays more? Why?
Some people argue that working while studying teaches valuable skills that classes cannot. Others say it distracts students from learning. What do you think?
Should universities limit the number of hours their students are allowed to work during the semester? Explain your position.

exercises.scenario: You are being interviewed for a campus podcast about learning and memory.

questions.prompt: Tell me about a skill you learned outside school. How did you go about learning it?
When you prepare for an important exam, do you prefer to study a little every day or in a few long sessions? Why?
Many people believe that memorizing information is less important now that we can look everything up online. Do you agree?
If you could change one thing about how universities assess students, what would it be, and what effect do you think it would have?
